doc.title: Ray Blue interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 23, 2022

title: Studio time, mixing and working with Bobby Sanabria
summary: Blue starts with ten-hour studio blocks, mixes with only engineer and producer, and describes Bobby Sanabria's perfectionist percussion overdubs.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: What’s the average time — I don’t know if you can estimate this but on your own recordings how much studio time do you usually get?

Well I would start out with probably a ten hour block. And then work it from there. Some folks go in and then they say all right I’m going to record all the tracks. The way I prefer to do it is that we’ll do as many tracks as it feels good with. You know? If the energy dissipates or something and it’s time to stop then we stop and then come back. Yeah. That’s it. I’ll start with ten hours and then we have time to go over a couple of things if we feel like it you know, at the end you do a listening and you say yeah well I’d like to do that a little differently and we’ll do it again, do a track again. But when it’s there you hear it and you know it and then you can move on to the next.
When it comes time to mix are the other members around or do you find it better to have as few people as possible in on that process?
No, no, I’m not having any other cats. Everybody hears their own.
Everybody wants to push up their fader.
You know yeah. It’s the engineer, producer and myself. That’s enough. Yeah. Funny. You know how that goes.
No one ever says hey I think I’m a little too loud.

Yeah. On this most recent recording I called in Bobby Sanabria to lay some tracks. And Bobby is another phenomenal one. Wow. Wow. And then he’d come in, I gave him, I sent him the music ahead of time and he came in with his notes and the markings on the pages and then he goes in and he made his track. He came in and listened and said hmmm, and he could pinpoint certain things, and go back and bam, he’ll hit it and it’s done. And then he said all right now I hear this to go in and he’ll have another percussive instrument. Etcetera. And then when we did the final listen before he leaves, you know, I love you Bobby, but we have to do it, “Yeah okay Bobby, sure Bobby, yeah Bobby.” “Add a little of this,” “Okay Bobby.” But he’s right and so it makes sense because you know, you fine tune. But what he does is he’s hearing these things and they’re really fine points, usable points. And so when it came time to start the mixing, bam, it was in there and all we had to do was fine tune it. You know? The “yeah-yeah” came because Bobby had so much energy. He goes on and on because he’s a perfectionist and he hears everything. You know he hears how it works with the drummer, where the accent is falling with the bass player, you know, on which beat of the measure or which subdivision part of the measure, where the piano player is rhythmically playing so that what he’s doing, it works to enhance. Because that’s his job. You know. So yeah, that was great working with him as well.
